nameStory: The Great Horned Owl gets its name from the prominent feather tufts on its head that look like horns or ears, though they're not actually ears at all! Early naturalists were so impressed by this owl's fierce hunting prowess that they called it the "winged tiger" or "tiger of the air," which is why it's sometimes still called the tiger owl today.
description: The Great Horned Owl is a large, powerful owl with distinctive "ear" tufts that stick up from its round head like horns. These impressive birds have a stocky build with broad wings and can grow quite large, making them one of the most formidable owls in New England. Their plumage is mottled brown and gray with intricate barring patterns, and they have piercing yellow eyes that seem to stare right through you. You're most likely to hear their deep, resonant hooting calls echoing through the night.

idTips.label: Feather Tufts
idTips.description: Two prominent feather tufts stick up from the head like cat ears or devil horns, spaced widely apart and quite noticeable even from a distance

idTips.label: Yellow Eyes
idTips.description: Bright yellow or golden eyes that appear to glow in low light, surrounded by distinctive facial discs with darker borders

idTips.label: Hooting Call
idTips.description: Deep, resonant "hoo-hoo-hoo, hoo-hoo" that carries far through the night air, with a rhythm like "Who's awake? Me too!"

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Large and stocky with broad wings, noticeably bigger than most other owls you'll see in New England, with a barrel-shaped body

idTips.label: Plumage Pattern
idTips.description: Complex mottled pattern of browns, grays, and buff colors with fine barring that provides excellent camouflage against tree bark

idTips.label: White Throat Patch
idTips.description: Bright white bib or throat patch that's especially visible when the owl is calling, contrasting sharply with the darker surrounding feathers

habitat: Great Horned Owls are incredibly adaptable and can be found throughout New England in almost any habitat with trees for roosting and nesting. Look for them in mixed forests, suburban areas with mature trees, swamps, parks, and even urban areas near wooded sections. They prefer areas with a mix of open hunting grounds and dense cover, from sea level to mountainous regions.

seasonality.spring: Peak nesting season when you might hear frequent territorial hooting and see adults carrying prey to young. Listen for begging calls from juveniles in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Adults are quieter as they focus on raising young, but recently fledged juveniles may be visible begging for food with harsh screeching calls.
seasonality.fall: Young owls disperse to find their own territories, making this a good time to spot them in unusual places. Hooting begins to increase as winter approaches.
seasonality.winter: Most vocal period with frequent territorial hooting on clear, cold nights. One of the few birds actively nesting in late winter, often taking over hawk or crow nests.

funFact: Great Horned Owls are one of the few animals brave enough to regularly hunt skunks, and they're so successful at it that skunk remains are commonly found in their nests - apparently their poor sense of smell means the spray doesn't bother them at all!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Long-eared Owls, but Great Horned Owls are much larger with wider-spaced ear tufts and yellow (not orange) eyes. Remember: Great Horned = Great big with Great big yellow eyes, while Long-eared are smaller, slimmer, and have orange eyes with closely-spaced ear tufts.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "horns" and sometimes mistaken for ears, those feather tufts are neither - they're just decorative plumes! The owl's actual ears are hidden asymmetrically on the sides of its head, which helps with pinpoint hearing for hunting.
compareHints: While the Snowy Owl is the only other species in the same genus found in New England, Great Horned Owls are easily distinguished by their prominent ear tufts, brown and gray mottled plumage, and year-round presence. Snowy Owls lack ear tufts entirely, are predominantly white, and only visit during winter months. Great Horned Owls are also more likely to be found in wooded areas, while Snowy Owls prefer open fields and shorelines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to their closest New England relative, the great horned owl, snowy owls are easily distinguished by their white plumage and lack of 'ear tufts' (the horn-like feather projections).
